chapters.title: Chapter 3: When Country Risk Turns Into Crisis

lessons.title: Currency Crises and Capital Flight: How Country Risk Hits Ordinary Investors

children.text: Sri Lanka's default was a headline about bondholders and restructuring negotiations. The fuel queues, medicine shortages, and power cuts that actually defined daily life during the crisis were about something more immediate: a currency in freefall. This lesson traces exactly how a currency crisis and capital flight move from a trading screen to an ordinary person's grocery bill, electricity connection, and investment portfolio.
What a Currency Crisis Actually Is

markDefs.definition: A sudden, sharp, and disorderly loss of a currency's value, typically after a central bank has spent down reserves trying to defend a fixed or managed exchange rate and is finally forced to let it go.

children.text: is not the same thing as ordinary currency volatility. The rupee moving 1 to 2% against the dollar over a few weeks is normal market noise, the kind of movement India's managed float, covered in Chapter 2, absorbs routinely. A currency crisis is a different animal: a rapid, often 30 to 60% or larger, loss of value over months, usually because a central bank has been artificially propping the currency up and finally runs out of ammunition to keep doing so. Sri Lanka's rupee, defended for months before being floated in March 2022, is the exact pattern this lesson is built around.
The Transmission Mechanism: From Capital Flight to Your Wallet

markDefs.definition: A rapid, large-scale withdrawal of investment capital from a country by foreign (and sometimes domestic) investors, typically triggered by a loss of confidence in the country's economic or political stability.

children.text: The mechanism runs in a fairly consistent sequence once

begins in earnest. Foreign (and often domestic) investors start selling local bonds and equities and converting the proceeds into dollars to move out of the country. That selling pressure pushes the local currency down. To slow the fall, the central bank sells its own dollar reserves to buy the local currency, which is exactly the reserve depletion pattern from the last two lessons. If outflows continue, reserves eventually run too thin to keep defending the rate, and the currency is forced to float or is sharply devalued, often overnight. From there, the effects spread well beyond the trading floor.

body.caption: How a Currency Crisis Reaches Ordinary People

cells: Imported goods priced in dollars, fuel, cooking gas, edible oil, medicine, become far more expensive in local currency terms almost overnight
The country may simply be unable to pay for enough fuel or medicine imports, leading to physical shortages and queues, exactly what Sri Lanka experienced in 2022
The central bank raises interest rates sharply to defend the currency and control inflation
Loans, mortgages, and business borrowing costs rise quickly, squeezing households and companies with variable-rate debt
The government may impose capital controls as a last resort
Ordinary citizens, students paying foreign tuition, families sending remittances, travellers, can face real restrictions on converting or moving money abroad

body.text: Imported inflation is often the fastest and most painful transmission channel. A country does not need to import much, relative to GDP, for a currency collapse to hurt badly, if what it does import is essential and price-inelastic, like fuel, cooking gas, or life-saving medicine. Sri Lanka imports the vast majority of its fuel; when the rupee collapsed, the local-currency cost of every litre spiked immediately, which is exactly why fuel queues, not abstract bond market charts, became the defining image of the crisis.

children.text: The Investor Angle: When a Local Gain Becomes a Dollar Loss

Foreign investors experience currency crises through a specific, often underestimated mechanic: a local-currency gain can turn into a dollar-denominated loss the moment the currency collapses, because the two returns compound against each other rather than simply adding up.

body.caption: The approximate return a foreign investor actually earns in dollars combines the local-currency return with the currency's move against the dollar. A weakening local currency (negative FX return) can erase, or reverse, a positive local gain.

children.text: Work through an illustrative example. Suppose a foreign investor holds a stock listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange that rises 20% in rupee terms over a year, a genuinely good local return. Over that same year, the rupee depreciates 50% against the dollar. The investor's dollar return is not simply 20% minus 50%. It is (1.20) multiplied by (1 minus 0.50), minus 1, which works out to a loss of roughly 40%. A 20% local gain turned into a 40% dollar loss, purely through currency translation, without the investor's underlying holding changing at all in rupee terms.

body.title: Calculate the Dollar Return
body.prompt: A foreign investor's local-currency equity holding gains 15% over a year. Over the same period, the local currency depreciates 40% against the dollar. Using the approximation from this lesson, what is the investor's approximate dollar-denominated return, in percent? (Enter a negative number if it is a loss.)
body.explanation: (1 + 0.15) multiplied by (1 minus 0.40), minus 1, equals 1.15 multiplied by 0.60, minus 1, which is 0.69 minus 1, or approximately -31%. Even a healthy 15% local gain is wiped out and turned into a roughly 31% dollar loss once a 40% currency depreciation is layered on top, which is exactly why foreign investors treat currency risk as inseparable from the underlying investment return, not an afterthought.

children.text: How Central Banks Try to Defend a Currency (and Why It Often Fails)

markDefs.definition: Government restrictions on the ability to convert local currency into foreign currency or move money across borders, typically imposed during a crisis to slow capital flight and stabilise reserves.

children.text: Central banks have three main levers once outflow pressure builds, and each has real limits. Direct intervention, selling dollars from reserves to buy the local currency, works immediately but burns down a finite stockpile, exactly the mechanism that drained Sri Lanka's reserves before the 2022 float. Raising interest rates sharply makes holding the local currency more attractive by offering a higher return, but it also raises borrowing costs for every domestic business and household with a loan, and can choke off growth precisely when the economy can least afford it.

, restricting how much money can leave the country, are usually the last resort, and while they can buy time, they also damage investor confidence for years afterward, since investors who could not get their money out during one crisis tend to price that risk into every future decision about that country. There is no clean, costless way to defend a currency once the underlying vulnerabilities described in the last two lessons have already built up. The defense can only buy time, not fix the underlying problem.

body.title: Weighing the Central Bank's Options
body.scenario: A country's currency is under sustained selling pressure after a sovereign rating downgrade. Its central bank is deciding between three options: (1) continue selling reserves to defend the current exchange rate, (2) raise interest rates sharply, or (3) let the currency float freely and absorb the depreciation.
body.prompt: What is the key trade-off the central bank faces, and why might delaying a decision (option 1, continued defense) often make the eventual outcome worse rather than better?
body.modelAnswer: Each option trades one form of pain for another: continued reserve defense preserves currency stability today but depletes the buffer needed to handle future shocks or pay for essential imports; raising rates defends the currency but slows growth and raises domestic borrowing costs; floating the currency accepts an immediate, visible depreciation but stops the reserve bleed and lets the exchange rate find a market-clearing level. Delaying the decision by continuing to defend an unsustainable rate is often the worst outcome, because it burns through reserves that could otherwise cushion the eventual adjustment or fund essential imports, meaning the country arrives at the same eventual devaluation, but with even less capacity left to manage it, which is close to what happened in Sri Lanka before its March 2022 float.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why is imported inflation often the fastest way a currency crisis reaches ordinary people, even in a country that does not import a huge share of its GDP?
options: Imported inflation only affects luxury goods, which few people buy
If the specific goods imported are essential and price-inelastic, like fuel or medicine, their local-currency cost rises immediately and cannot easily be avoided by consumers
Imported inflation always takes several years to filter through to consumers
Currency depreciation only affects exporters, not importers
body.explanation: What matters is not just how much a country imports relative to GDP, but what it imports. Fuel, cooking gas, and medicine are essentials that most households and businesses cannot simply stop buying when prices rise, so a currency collapse pushes their local-currency cost up almost immediately, and that pain shows up fast and visibly, exactly as it did in Sri Lanka's fuel and medicine queues.

body.text: A currency crisis does not stay confined to a trading screen. It travels from capital flight, to reserve depletion, to a currency collapse, to the price of fuel and medicine on a shop shelf, in a matter of weeks. For a foreign investor, it can also travel straight into a portfolio, turning a genuinely good local return into a real dollar loss.

children.text: When a country reaches the point Sri Lanka reached in 2022, out of reserves and unable to defend its currency or service its debt on its own, it typically turns to one institution built specifically for this situation. The next lesson covers the IMF's role: what a bailout programme actually involves, what conditionality really means in practice, and why IMF programmes are simultaneously essential and deeply unpopular.

points: A currency crisis is a rapid, disorderly currency collapse, usually after a central bank has exhausted reserves defending an unsustainable rate, distinct from ordinary day-to-day currency volatility.

The transmission runs from capital flight, to reserve depletion, to a currency collapse, to imported inflation on essentials, to higher domestic interest rates, and sometimes to capital controls, each step reaching ordinary people more directly than the last.

Foreign investors face a compounding effect: dollar returns combine the local-currency return with the currency's move, so a real local gain can become a real dollar loss if the currency depreciates sharply enough.
Central banks have three main levers, reserve intervention, interest rate hikes, and capital controls, and each buys time at a real cost rather than solving the underlying vulnerability.
Delaying an unavoidable currency adjustment by continuing to defend an unsustainable rate often leaves a country with fewer resources to manage the eventual crisis, rather than preventing it.

body.text: The percentages and figures in this lesson's worked examples are simplified and illustrative, designed to teach the currency-translation mechanic clearly, not to represent live market data. Real-world currency and equity returns should be calculated from actual reported figures for any specific investment decision.
